# {{senseid|en|Q4022}}A large and often winding [[stream]] which drains a land mass, carrying water down from higher areas to a lower point, oftentimes ending in another body of water, such as an ocean or in an inland sea.
#: {{syn|en|Thesaurus:river}}
#: {{ux|en|Occasionally '''rivers''' overflow their [[bank]]s and cause floods.}}
#* {{RQ:Grahame Wind in the Willows|passage=By the side of the '''river''' he trotted as one trots, when very small, by the side of a man who holds one spell-bound by exciting stories; and when tired at last, he sat on the bank, while the '''river''' still chattered on to him, a babbling procession of the best stories in the world, sent from the heart of the earth to be told at last to the insatiable sea.}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-06-29|volume=407|issue=8842|page=28| title=High and wet|url=http://www.economist.com/news/asia/21580209-natural-disaster-aggravated-poor-response-high-and-wet| passage=Floods in northern India, mostly in the small state of Uttarakhand, have wrought disaster on an enormous scale. The early, intense onset of the monsoon on June 14th swelled '''rivers''', washing away roads, bridges, hotels and even whole villages. Rock-filled torrents smashed vehicles and homes, burying victims under rubble and sludge.}}
# Any large flow of a [[liquid]] in a single body.
#: {{ux|en|a '''river''' of blood}}
# {{senseid|en|poker}} {{lb|en|poker}} The last card [[deal|dealt]] in a [[hand]].
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2017|author=Nathan Schwiethale|title=Ace High: Mastering Low Stakes Poker Cash Games|page=70
|passage=He called instantly but was too ashamed to show until the '''river'''.}}
# {{lb|en|typography}} A visually undesirable effect of white space running down a page, caused by spaces between words on consecutive lines happening to coincide.

=====Usage notes=====
* As with the names of {{l|en|lake|lakes}} and {{l|en|mountain|mountains}}, the names of rivers are typically formed by adding the word before or after the unique term: the {{m|en|River Thames}} or the {{m|en|Yangtze River}}. Generally speaking, names formed using adjectives or attributives see ''river'' added to the end, as with the {{m|en|Yellow River}}. It is less common to add ''river'' before names than it is with lakes, but many of the rivers of Britain are written that way, as with the {{m|en|River Severn}}; indeed, British English tends to use "River X" in such cases while American, South African, Australian and New Zealand English use "X River". The former derives from the earlier but now uncommon form ''river of ~'': the 19th century ''River of Jordan'' is now usually simply the ''River Jordan''.
* It is common to preface the proper names of rivers with the article {{m|en|the}}.
* Concerning the reference of its coordinate terms, some people say:<ref>[http://worldrivers.net/2018/11/29/distinction-of-rivers-stream-brooks-creeks-and-other-terms/ Definitions of rivers, stream, brooks, creeks and other terms] (Goran Šafarek, ''WorldRivers.net,'' November 29, 2018)</ref> you can step over a {{m|en|brook}}, jump over a {{m|en|creek}}, wade across a {{m|en|stream}}, and swim across a {{m|en||river}}.

{{also|Field}} ==English== [[File:Fields below Frocester Hill (1565).jpg|thumb|right|'''Fields'''|360px]] ===Etymology=== {{root|en|ine-pro|*pleth₂-}} {{dercat|en|gmw-pro|inh=1}} {{etymon|en|:inh|enm:feld|tree=1}} From {{inh|en|enm|feld}}, {{m|enm|feeld||field}}, from {{inh|en|ang|feld||field}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*felþu||field}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*felþuz|t=field}}, ultimately from {{der|en|ine-pro|*pleh₂-|t=field, plain}} or {{m|ine-pro|*pleth₂-|t=flat}} (with [[schwebeablaut]]). {{col-top|2|cog}} Cognate with {{cog|sco|feld}}, {{m|sco|feild||field}}, {{cog|frr|fial}}, {{m|frr|fälj||field}}, {{cog|stq|Fäild||field}}, {{cog|fy|fjild||field}}, {{cog|nl|veld||field}}, {{cog|de,lb|Feld||field}}, {{cog|wym|fald||field}}, {{cog|da,nb,nn|felt|t=field}}, {{cog|sv|fält|t=field}}, {{cog|fi|pelto||field}}, {{cog|ast|-}} and {{cog|roa-leo|platu||plate}}, {{cog|an|-}} and {{cog|es|plato||plate}}, {{cog|ca|plat||plate}}, {{cog|fr|plat||dish}}, {{cog|gl|-}}, {{cog|mwl|-}}, and {{cog|pt|prato||plate}}, {{cog|it|piatto||plate}}, {{cog|la|*plattus||flattened}}, {{cog|el|πλατύς||wide, broad}}. Doublet of {{m|en|plate}}. Related also to {{cog|enm|flat||flat}}, {{cog|ang|folde||earth, land, territory}}, {{cog|ang|folm||palm of the hand}}. More at ''[[flat]]'', ''[[fold]]''. Not related to {{ncog|en|felt}}. {{col-bottom}} ===Pronunciation=== * {{IPA|en|/ˈfi(ː)ld/|[ˈfɪi̯ɫd]}} ** {{audio|en|en-us-field.ogg|a=GA}} ** {{audio|en|en-au-field.ogg|a=AU}} *** {{IPA|en|/ˈfi(ː)ʊ̯d/|[ˈfɪi̯ʊd]|a=l-vocalization}} * {{rhymes|en|iːld|s=1}} * {{hyph|en|field}} * {{homophones|en|feeled}} ===Noun=== {{en-noun}} # {{senseid|en|land area free of woodland, cities, and towns; open country}} A land area free of [[woodland]], cities, and towns; an area of open country. #: {{ux|en|There are several species of wild flowers growing in this '''field'''.}} ## {{lb|en|usually|in the plural}} The open country near or belonging to a town or city. ##* {{quote-book|en|author=w:Anthony Trollope|title=Mr. Scarborough's Family|year=1883|section=Chap. XXIV|passage=Harry shook his head, and wandered away miserable through the '''fields''', and would not in these days even set his foot upon the soil of the park. “He was not going to intrude any farther,” he said to the rector. “You can come to church, at any rate,” his father said, “for he certainly will not be there while you are at the parsonage.” Oh yes, Harry would go to the church. “I have yet to understand that Mr. Prosper is owner of the church, and the path there from the rectory is, at any rate, open to the public;” for at Buston the church stands on one corner of the park.}} ##* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=8|passage=I corralled the judge, and we started off across the '''fields''', in no very mild state of fear of that gentleman's wife, whose vigilance was seldom relaxed. And thus we came by a circuitous route to Mohair, the judge occupied by his own guilty thoughts, and I by others not less disturbing.}} # {{senseid|en|wide, open space used to grow crops or to hold farm animals}} A wide, open space that is used to grow [[crop]]s or to hold [[farm]] [[animal]]s, usually enclosed by a fence, hedge or other barrier. #: {{ux|en|There were some cows grazing in a '''field'''.}} #: {{ux|en|A crop circle was made in a corn '''field'''.}} #* {{quote-book|en|author=w:Lord Byron|title=w:Childe Harold's Pilgrimage|section=Canto the Third, LV|year=1816|passage=The castled crag of Drachenfels
Frowns o’er the wide and winding Rhine
Whose breast of waters broadly swells

And hills all rich with blossomed trees
And '''fields''' which promise corn and wine

Have strew’d a scene, which I should see

Penny] |chapter=5|title=Pulling the Strings |url=http://openlibrary.org/works/OL16814587W |passage=Anstruther laughed good-naturedly. “[…] I shall take out half a dozen intelligent maistries from our Press and get them to give our villagers instruction when they begin work and when they are in the '''fields'''.”}} ## {{non-gloss|When coupled with a number (e.g. two-field) used to define types of [[crop rotation]], denoting the number of different [[crop]] types (and possibly [[fallow]]) that are used}}. # {{senseid|en|geology: region containing a particular mineral}}{{lb|en|geology}} A region containing a particular mineral. #: {{ux|en|an oil '''field'''; a gold '''field'''}} # An [[airfield]], [[airport]] or [[air base]]; especially, one with unpaved [[runway]]s. # A place where [[competitive]] [[match]]es are carried out. ## {{senseid|en|place where a battle is fought}} A place where a [[battle]] is fought; a [[battlefield]]. ##* {{quote-book|en|year=c. 1599|author=w:William Shakespeare|title={{w|Henry V (play)|King Henry V}}|section=act IV, scene VI|passage=Tarry, sweet soul, for mine; then fly abreast,
As in this glorious and well-foughten '''field'''
We kept together in our chivalry!}} ##* {{quote-book|en|year=1674|author=w:John Milton|title=w:Paradise Lost|passage=[…] What though the '''field''' be lost?
All is not lost; th’ unconquerable will,
And study of revenge, immortal hate,
And courage never to submit or yield,
And what is else not to be overcome;
That glory never shall his wrath or might!|section=Book 1, Verses 105–110}} ## {{senseid|en|sports: area reserved for playing a game}} An area reserved for playing a game or race with one’s physical force. ##: {{ux|en|soccer '''field'''}} ##: {{ux|en|Substitutes are only allowed onto the '''field''' after their boots are checked.}} ##* {{quote-book|en|author=w:Anthony Trollope|title=The Kellys and the O’Kellys|year=1848|section=Chap. III|passage=Blake was a thorough gambler, and knew well how to make the most of the numerous chances which the turf afforded him. He had a large stud of horses, to the training and working of which he attended almost as closely as the person whom he paid for doing so. But it was in the betting-ring that he was most formidable. It was said, in Kildare Street, that no one at Tattersall's could beat him at a book. ===Etymology 1===
[[File:Glarus Kloentalersee.jpg|thumb|A mountain lake.]]
{{ety|en|id=body of water|:inh|enm:lake<ety:inh<ang:lacu>>|enm:lac<ety:bor<fro:lac>>|tree=1}}
Arose from a conflation of

* {{inh|en|enm|lake|t=small stream of running water, pool, lake}}, from {{inh|en|ang|lacu|t=stream, pool, pond, lake}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*laku}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*lakō|t=stream, pool, body of water", originally "a place where water runs off and collects}}, ultimately from {{der|en|ine-pro|*leg-|t=to leak, drain}}; with
* {{noncog|enm|lac|t=lake}}, from {{noncog|fro|lac|t=lake, ditch, pit}}, a borrowed term, likely from {{noncog|la|lacus|t=lake, tub, vat}} (see {{m+|fro|lac}} for more).

The first element is related to {{cog|nl|laak|t=stream, drainage ditch, pond}}, {{cog|nds-de|Lake}}, {{m|nds-de|Laak|t=drainage, marshland}}, {{cog|de|Lache|t=puddle, pool}}, {{cog|no|løk|t=a deep, slow-moving stream; a widening in a stream or river}}, {{cog|fo|løkur|t=small brook}} and {{m|fo|lækja|t=water hole, well, watershoot in a brook}}, {{cog|is|lækur|t=stream}}.<ref>{{R:OED Online|code=105167|entry=lake|pos=n.3|date=September 2021}}</ref>

Despite their similarity in form and meaning, {{m+|ang|lacu}} is not related to {{noncog|en|lay#Etymology_2|t=lake}}, {{noncog|la|lacus|t=hollow, lake, pond}}, {{noncog|gd|loch|t=lake}}, {{noncog|grc|λάκκος|t=waterhole, tank, pond, pit}}, all from {{noncog|ine-pro|*lókus|*lókus, *l̥kwés|t=lake, pool}}.<ref>{{R:gem:EDPG|head=Lagu-}}</ref>

====Noun====
{{en-noun}}

# {{senseid|en|Q23397}}A large, landlocked stretch of [[water]] or similar liquid.
#* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=4|passage=Judge Short had gone to town, and Farrar was off for a three days' cruise up the '''lake'''. I was bitterly regretting I had not gone with him when the distant notes of a coach horn reached my ear, and I descried a four-in-hand winding its way up the inn road from the direction of Mohair.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=2015-07-31|author=|title=Morphologically Cryptic Amphipod Species Are “Ecological Clones” at Regional but Not at Local Scale: A Case Study of Four Niphargus Species|journal=PLOS ONE|url=http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0134384|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0134384|volume=|issue=|pages=
|passage=These included other ''Niphargus'' species from deep cave '''lakes''' and coastal anchihaline caves [23 ] and ''Gammarus'' and ''Echinogammarus'' amphipods that live only in permanently watered streams [21 ,24 ].}}
# A large amount of [[liquid]].
#: {{syn|en|mountain}}
#: {{ux|en|a '''lake''' of wine}}
#: {{ux|en|A '''lake''' of hot grease covered the floor by the stove.}}
#* '''1991''', {{w|Robert DeNiro}} (actor), ''{{w|Backdraft (film)|Backdraft}}'':
#*: So you punched out a window for ventilation. Was that ''before'' or ''after'' you noticed you were standing in a '''lake''' of gasoline?
# {{lb|en|now|chiefly|dialectal}} A small [[stream]] of running [[water]]; a [[channel]] for water; a [[drain]].
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} A [[pit]], or [[ditch]].

=====Usage notes=====
* As with the names of {{m|en|[[river]]s}}, {{m|en|[[mount]]s}} and {{m|en|[[mountain]]s}}, the names of lakes are typically formed by adding the word before or after the unique term: {{m|en|Lake Titicaca}} or {{m|en|Great Slave Lake}}. Generally speaking, names formed using adjectives or attributives see {{m|en||lake}} added to the end, as with {{m|en|Reindeer Lake}}; {{m|en||lake}} is usually added before proper names, as with {{m|en|Lake Michigan}}. This derives from the earlier but now uncommon form {{m|en||lake of ~}}: for instance, the 19th-century {{m|en|Lake of Annecy}} is now usually simply {{m|en|Lake Annecy}}. There are exceptions to this generalization, however, including notably the names of the individual [[Finger Lakes]] (e.g. [[Oneida]] Lake, [[Seneca]] Lake, [[Cayuga]] Lake). It frequently occurs, however, that foreign placenames are misunderstood as proper nouns, as with the Chinese {{m|en|Taihu||Great Lake}} and {{m|en|Qinghai||Blue Sea}} being frequently rendered as {{m|en|Lake Tai}} and {{m|en|Qinghai Lake}}.

=====Usage notes=====
* When used in the sense "from one location to another", ''over'' implies that the two places are at approximately the same height or the height difference is not relevant. For example, if two offices are on the same floor of a building, an office worker might say ''I'll bring that '''over''' for you'', while if the offices were on different floors, the sentence would likely be ''I'll bring that up [down] for you.'' However, distances are not constrained, e.g. ''He came '''over''' from England last year and now lives in Los Angeles'' or ''I moved the stapler '''over''' to the other side of my desk.''

===Etymology 1===
{{etymon|en|id=adjective|:inh|enm:fre|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|fre}}, from {{inh|en|ang|frēo}}, {{m|ang|frēoh}}, {{m|ang|frī}}, {{m|ang|friġ}}, {{m|ang|frīoh|t=free}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*frī}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*frijaz|t=beloved, not in bondage}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*priHós|t=pleased, loved}}, from {{m|ine-pro|*preyH-|t=to please; to love}}. Related to {{m|en|friend}}.
{{box-top|cognates, etc}}
Germanic cognates include {{cog|sco|fre|t=free}}, {{cog|frr|frai}}, {{m|frr|frei}}, {{m|frr|fri}}, {{m|frr|Frii|t=free}}, {{cog|stq|fräi|t=free}}, {{cog|fy|frij|t=free}}, {{cog|nl|vrij|t=free}}, {{cog|de|frei|t=free}}, {{cog|nds|free|t=free}}, {{cog|lb|fräi|t=free}}, {{cog|wym|frȧj|t=free}}, {{cog|yi|פֿרײַ|t=free}}, {{cog|da,nb,nn,sv|fri|t=free}}, {{cog|fo|fríur|t=free}}, {{cog|got|𐍆𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃|t=free}}.

Other cognates include {{cog|kw|rydh|t=free}}, {{cog|cy|rhydd|t=free}}, {{cog|la|propriō|t=to appropriate}}, {{cog|cs|přát|t=to wish; to favour}}, {{cog|pl|sprzyjać|t=to favour, foster}}, {{cog|sh|прѝјати}}, {{m|sh|prìjati|t=to please, taste, suit; to be agreeable, relish}}, {{cog|sk|priať|t=to wish}}, {{cog|ae|𐬟𐬭𐬌𐬌𐬀|t=good, pleasant}}, {{cog|fa|فری|tr=fari|t=beloved, dear; agreeable, pleasing}}, {{cog|sa|प्रिय|t=beloved}}.

Germanic and Celtic are the only Indo-European language branches in which the PIE word with the meaning of "dear, beloved" acquired the additional meaning of "free" in the sense of "not in bondage". This was an extension of the idea of "characteristic of those who are dear and beloved", in other words friends and tribe members (in contrast to unfree inhabitants from other tribes and prisoners of war, many of which were among the slaves – compare the Latin use of [[liberi]] to mean both "free persons" and "children of a family").<ref>{{R:Etymonline}}</ref><ref>[https://www.dwds.de/wb/frei "frei"] in Digitales Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache</ref>
